sections.h: The outer flow waits in flatMapConcat, and flatMapLatest drops the old lane
sections.body:
A merchant search box gets three picks, 100 ms apart. For each pick, a details flow sends part a after 50 ms and part b 150 ms later. With `flatMapConcat`, at what time does the outer flow emit pick 2?

```kotlin
picks().flatMapConcat { n -> details(n) }     // also try flatMapMerge and flatMapLatest
```

```java
// Closest Java equivalent: concatMap (and flatMap, switchMap) on the same Flux timeline
picks().concatMap(n -> details(n));
```

Most people say 100. It is 300, and the whole run takes 800 ms. `flatMapConcat` is `map(transform).flattenConcat()`, and `flattenConcat` is one line: `collect { value -> emitAll(value) }`. No coroutine, no channel. The inner flow runs inside the outer's `emit`, so the outer's code is paused until the inner has finished, and its `delay(100)` only starts after that. Picture a single-lane bridge where the depot worker drives each truck across himself. No new truck gets loaded while one is on the bridge. Put `buffer()` in front, and the outer runs in its own coroutine and loads trucks into a parking lot. The run drops to 600 ms.

Reactor's `concatMap` on the same timeline also finishes at 600 ms. It asks for one item at a time too, but the timers in its source kept running while no request was outstanding. A `flow { }` body can't do that: it is suspended in `emit`. If you want Reactor's timeline in Flow, add the `buffer()`.

`flatMapMerge` gives each pick its own lane. The outer emits at 0, 100 and 200, the inner values interleave by completion time (1-b at 200 comes after 2-a at 150), and the run ends at 400.

`flatMapLatest` is a railway switch that drops the old lane. It is `transformLatest { emitAll(transform(it)) }`, the operator from lesson 4 of this track. Each new pick cancels the inner in flight with `ChildCancelledException` ("Child of the scoped flow was cancelled"), joins it, and starts the next. So 1-b and 2-b never arrive, and the run ends at 400. Reactor's `switchMap` gives the identical timeline. This is the shape for search-as-you-type: a new keystroke makes the old search worthless. Keep the cancelled inner's cleanup short, because the next one waits for it.

The figure shows all three, drawn from the virtual-time output of the Try it.

Check yourself: the outer is `for (n in 1..3) { emit(n); delay(100) }` and each inner is one value after 200 ms. How long does `flatMapConcat` take?

sections.h: A zipper for zip, a board of latest values for combine
sections.body:
Checkout prices arrive in USD every 100 ms, starting at 100 ms. The USD to EUR rate arrives at 250 ms (0.92) and at 550 ms (0.95). You want each price in EUR. A teammate writes `prices.zip(rates)`:

```kotlin
prices.zip(rates) { cents, rate -> EurPrice(cents, rate) }       // a zipper
combine(prices, rates) { cents, rate -> EurPrice(cents, rate) }  // a board of latest values
merge(cardEvents, bankEvents)                                     // on-ramps onto one road
```

```java
// Closest Java equivalent: the same three Reactor operators
Flux.zip(prices, rates, EurPrice::new);
Flux.combineLatest(prices, rates, EurPrice::new);
Flux.merge(cardEvents, bankEvents);
```

`zip` gives two results: 1000 at 0.92 at 250 ms, and 1010 at 0.95 at 550 ms. Then it ends. It is a zipper: each price tooth must meet a rate tooth, by index, and it stops at the end of the shorter side. The price flow's `onCompletion` reports `AbortFlowException: Flow was aborted, no more elements needed`. Something else happened too: the second price was emitted at 350 ms, not 200. `zip` collects the receiver (`prices`) in the caller's coroutine with no buffer at all, and only the other flow gets a producer coroutine with a rendezvous channel. So each price `emit` waits until a rate is there to pair with. The slower side sets the pace. Reactor's `zip` produced the same two pairs, but its price feed kept ticking every 100 ms, because Reactor prefetches. Flow has only the two-flow `zip`.

Pairing the n-th price with the n-th rate is the wrong question for money. You want the latest rate. That is `combine`, which keeps a board with one slot per flow. It starts one coroutine per source. Nothing comes out until every slot has a value, and after that every update produces one output. The first result is 1010 at 0.92, at 250 ms: price 1000 was overwritten on the board before any rate existed. Then 1020, 1030 and 1040 at 0.92, then 1040 at 0.95 the moment the new rate lands at 550, then 1050 at 0.95. A source that never emits means no output at all, and `combine` completes when the other sources complete.

`merge` is on-ramps joining one road. Card events every 100 ms and bank events every 70 ms come out in arrival order: bank-0 at 70, card-0 at 100, bank-1 at 140, and so on. The merged flow ends when the last source ends, and one source that fails cancels the others.

Check yourself: what does `combine` emit if the rate flow sends 0.92 at 0 ms, before the first price?

sections.h: A slow collector makes combine skip values and slow its sources
sections.body:
Put a slow collector behind `combine`. A price feed ticks every 10 ms, ten times, and is combined with one merchant config value. The dashboard that collects the result needs 100 ms per update. What does it see?

```kotlin
combine(ticks, flowOf("cfg")) { i, cfg -> "$i/$cfg" }
    .collect { render(it); delay(100) }        // the dashboard is slow
```

```java
// Closest Java equivalent: combineLatest in front of a subscriber that takes one at a time
Flux.combineLatest(ticks, Flux.just("cfg"), (i, cfg) -> i + "/" + cfg)
    .concatMap(v -> render(v).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(100)), 1);
```

Flow delivers 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 10, at 10, 110, 210, 310, 410 and 510 ms. Reactor's `combineLatest` delivers all ten, at about 110, 210 and so on up to 1,010 ms. And there is a second effect in Flow: the feed itself slowed down. It needed about 330 ms to emit its ten values, not 100.

The mechanism is the board's mailbox. Each source coroutine sends an update into a channel whose capacity equals the number of flows, here 2, and then calls `yield()`. The collecting loop takes updates in batches: it reads until it sees a second update from a source it already updated in this batch, overwriting that source's slot each time, and then calls your transform once for the batch. While the dashboard is busy, updates pile up. 2 is overwritten by 3 before anyone takes a photo of the board. Once the mailbox is full, the feed's next `send` suspends: value 4 waits in `send` from 40 ms. So `combine` backpressures its sources and skips values, both at once. Picture a scoreboard and a slow photographer. Updates that land between two photos blur into the last one, and the mailbox in front of the board holds only as many notes as there are slots, so fast sources queue at the mailbox. Reactor's photographer keeps every board state in a queue and develops them all.

It is not plain conflation either. Pure latest-only would give 1 and then 10. If you care, say which one you want:

| After `combine(...)` | The dashboard sees |
|---|---|
| nothing | 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 10 and the feed slows |
| `.conflate()` | 1 at 10 ms, then 10 at 110 ms |
| `.buffer(Channel.UNLIMITED)` | all ten, the last at 1,010 ms |

For FX on a dashboard, skipping is fine. For anything you must audit, every combination counts, and an unbounded buffer is a memory bill you must size yourself.

One more thing not to rely on. Two flows with no delays, `combine(flowOf("a0", "a1", "a2"), flowOf("b0", "b1", "b2"))`, give `a0b0, a1b1, a2b2` in Flow and `a2b0, a2b1, a2b2` in Reactor. With synchronous sources, the combinations you get depend on scheduling.

Check yourself: with the dashboard at 100 ms per update, would `buffer(10)` instead of `UNLIMITED` keep all ten?

refs.title: internal/Combine.kt at tag 1.11.0 (how combine and zip are built)

analogy: Think of road traffic. `flatMapConcat` is a single-lane bridge where the depot worker drives every truck across himself, so the depot stops loading while a truck is on the bridge. `flatMapMerge` is a toll plaza: one dispatcher waves cars in one at a time, N booths work in parallel, and cars leave in the order they finish. `flatMapLatest` is a railway switch that sends the old train to a siding the moment a new one comes, and waits for the old one to stop. `zip` is a zipper, tooth for tooth. `combine` is a scoreboard with one slot per source. `merge` is on-ramps joining a highway. The picture breaks at speed: real traffic has no backpressure. On a Flow road, a slow collector at the end makes the cars upstream stop, and for `combine` it also blurs some cars into one.
in_your_world: Your payment service enriches each authorization with the merchant's fee schedule from a pricing service that allows 4 concurrent calls per client. `flatMapMerge(concurrency = 4) { m -> flow { emit(pricing.lookup(m)) }.catch { emit(defaultFee(m)) } }` respects that contract and keeps one 503 from cancelling the other lookups. The checkout page converts the basket into the customer's currency with `combine(basketTotals, fxRates)`, never `zip`, because the latest rate is what you quote. The merchant search box uses `flatMapLatest` so a stale query can't overwrite a fresh one. And the reconciliation job that merges card-network and bank events uses `merge`, knowing that one feed failing stops both.
mistake: Putting the slow suspend call in the `flatMapMerge` lambda and returning `flowOf(result)`. It looks concurrent and it compiles without a warning, but the lambda runs in the single coroutine that reads the outer flow, before a lane is taken, so the calls happen one at a time. People make the mistake because Reactor's `flatMap` reads the same way and the code looks like a map with a cap. In both libraries the fix is the same: the slow work goes inside the returned flow or publisher, `flow { emit(lookup(m)) }` in Kotlin, `Mono.fromCallable` or a non-blocking client call in Reactor. If you need one result per item and no concurrency, plain `map { lookup(it) }` is simpler, and the `flatMapMerge` KDoc itself recommends it.

compare.title: Flattening and combining in Kotlin Flow and in Reactor

java.title: Reactor

kotlin.title: Kotlin Flow

compare.note: The operators line up one for one, and the virtual-time demos give the same timelines for `flatMap`/`flatMapMerge` and `switchMap`/`flatMapLatest`. The differences come from how each library moves values. In Flow, a value moves by a suspend call, so whatever is upstream of an `emit` waits for it: `flatMapConcat` pauses the outer's code (800 ms against Reactor's 600 on the same timeline), and `zip` slows its receiver to the other side's pace. Reactor moves values on demand and prefetches, so its sources keep their own timers. The defaults differ too: 16 lanes against 256. And with a slow subscriber, `combineLatest` queues every board state while `combine` skips some and makes its sources wait. Flow has no built-in `flatMapSequential`.

worked.title: Fan out fee lookups under a provider contract

steps.say: The pricing service allows 4 concurrent calls. Put the call inside the returned flow, so each merchant gets a lane, and set the cap from the contract. 10 lookups of 100 ms finish at 300 ms.

One merchant's lookup fails with a 503. Catch it inside that merchant's inner flow, so only that lane ends with a default. With m1 = 300, m2 = 100 (fails) and m3 = 200 ms, the output is m2's default at 100, m3 at 200 and m1 at 300.

Compare a `catch` placed after `flatMapMerge`. The failing lane cancels its siblings first: m1 and m3 end with `JobCancellationException` and the caller sees `IOException: fee service 503 for m2` at 100 ms. A caught error still ends the upstream, so the `catch` can only add a fallback after everything else was lost.
steps.code:
merchants.flatMapMerge(concurrency = 4) { m -> flow { emit(pricing.lookup(m)) } }
    .catch { e -> emit(defaultFee("all")) }      // too late: the other lanes are already cancelled

steps.say: The ledger wants the fees back in input order. Flow has no `flatMapSequential`. Start each call with `async`, keep up to n of them in flight with a buffer, and await them in order. The `buffer(n - 2)` counts the buffer's slots plus one `Deferred` being awaited and one being created, so n must be at least 2. 20 calls of 100 ms take 1,000 / 700 / 500 / 300 ms for n = 2 / 3 / 4 / 8, all in order.

drill.title: Write a capped fan-out from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write `fun <T, R> Flow<T>.mergeLanes(lanes: Int, transform: suspend (T) -> Flow<R>): Flow<R>` with `channelFlow`, a `Semaphore` and `launch`. Then answer: in your version, which line runs one value at a time, and why must the slow call not be in `transform`?

recap: `flatMapMerge` calls your lambda sequentially, in one producer coroutine, before it takes a lane. Only the returned flows run concurrently, so the slow call belongs inside them.
The cap defaults to 16 (`DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY`), against Reactor's 256. Set it from the provider's contract. Results come out in completion order.
`flatMapConcat` runs each inner inside the outer's `emit`, so the outer's own code pauses. `buffer()` in front lets it run ahead, which is Reactor's `concatMap` timeline.
`flatMapLatest` cancels the old inner, joins it and starts the new one. Use it for search-as-you-type, where stale results are worthless.

`zip` pairs by index, slows the receiver to the other side's pace and ends with the shorter flow. `combine` keeps the latest of each and emits once every source has a value. FX conversion is `combine`.
With a slow collector, `combine` skips intermediate values and suspends its sources. Add `conflate()` or `buffer()` to choose; Reactor's `combineLatest` keeps them all.

quiz.q:
Which call runs with up to 4 in flight?

```kotlin
merchants.flatMapMerge(4) { m ->
    val rules = rulesCache.load(m)               // suspends 50 ms
    flow { emit(pricing.lookup(m, rules)) }      // suspends 100 ms
}
```
options: Both: flatMapMerge makes the whole lambda concurrent
Only `pricing.lookup`; `rulesCache.load` runs one merchant at a time
Only `rulesCache.load`; the inner flow is collected later, one at a time
Neither, because `flow { }` inside a lambda is cold
quiz.why: The lambda runs in the one coroutine that reads the outer flow, sequentially and before a lane is taken. Only the returned flow gets a lane. So the 50 ms loads add up one after another, while the lookups overlap. Move the load into the inner flow if it should run concurrently too.

quiz.q: The outer is `flow { for (n in 1..3) { emit(n); delay(100) } }` and each inner is one value after 200 ms. `flatMapConcat` takes 900 ms. How long with `.buffer()` before `flatMapConcat`?
options: 600 ms
300 ms
800 ms
900 ms: buffer doesn't change a concat
quiz.why: Without the buffer, each inner runs inside the outer's `emit`, so the outer's `delay(100)` waits for it: 3 x (200 + 100). With the buffer, the outer runs ahead in its own coroutine and the three inners run back to back: 3 x 200 = 600 ms.

quiz.q: A checkout shows each basket total converted at the latest USD to EUR rate. The rate changes every few minutes; totals change whenever the customer edits the basket. Which operator fits?
options: `totals.zip(rates)`
`merge(totals, rates)`
`totals.flatMapLatest { rates }`
`combine(totals, rates)`
quiz.why: `combine` keeps the latest value of each flow and emits on every update of either, once both have a value. `zip` would pair the n-th total with the n-th rate and stall the totals until a new rate arrives. `merge` doesn't combine values at all. The `flatMapLatest` version restarts the rate flow on every basket edit and emits rates, not converted totals.

quiz.q: `combine(feed, flowOf("cfg"))` feeds a dashboard that needs 100 ms per update. The feed emits 1 to 10, 10 ms apart. What happens?
options: The dashboard sees all ten, 100 ms apart
The dashboard sees only 1 and 10
The dashboard sees 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 10, and the feed itself slows down
combine fails with an overflow error
quiz.why: `combine`'s mailbox holds one update per source. While the dashboard is busy, updates in the same batch overwrite each other, and once the mailbox is full the feed's `send` suspends. So it both skips and backpressures. All ten is Reactor's `combineLatest`, or Flow with `buffer(UNLIMITED)`. Only 1 and 10 is `conflate()`.

quiz.q: From the reactive track: on the same timeline, Reactor's `concatMap` finished at 600 ms and Kotlin's `flatMapConcat` at 800 ms. Why?
options: Reactor's concatMap prefetches 32 items
Flow's outer code is suspended inside `emit` while each inner runs, so its own delays start late; Reactor's source timers kept running
flatMapConcat runs the inners on Dispatchers.Default
Flow's flatMapConcat runs two inners at once
quiz.why: `flatMapConcat` is `collect { emitAll(it) }`: no coroutine and no channel, so the outer's body waits in `emit`. Reactor 3.8's `concatMap` requests one at a time too (no prefetch), but its source's `Mono.delay` timers ran while no request was outstanding. `buffer()` before `flatMapConcat` gives Flow the same 600 ms.

flashcards.front: In `flatMapMerge`, does the lambda run concurrently?
flashcards.back: No. It runs sequentially in the one coroutine that reads the outer flow, before a lane is taken. Only the flows it returns run concurrently.

flashcards.front: Default concurrency of `flatMapMerge`, and of Reactor's `flatMap`?
What happens to the outer flow while a `flatMapConcat` inner runs?
flashcards.back: Its code is paused inside `emit`: there is no extra coroutine or channel. `buffer()` before `flatMapConcat` lets it run ahead.

flashcards.front: `flatMapLatest` gets a new value while an inner is running. What happens?
flashcards.back: It cancels the inner with `ChildCancelledException`, joins it, then starts the inner for the new value.

flashcards.front: How does `zip` pair values, and when does it end?
flashcards.back: By index. It ends when the shorter flow ends and cancels the other. The receiver side has no buffer, so it waits for the other side.

flashcards.front: When does `combine` emit its first value?
flashcards.back: When every source has emitted at least once. After that, once per update of any source.

flashcards.front: `combine` with a slow collector: what happens to fast updates?
flashcards.back: Some are skipped (overwritten on the board) and the sources are suspended, since the mailbox holds one update per source. Reactor's `combineLatest` delivers them all.

terms.plain: Turning a flow of flows (one inner flow per outer value) into one flow of values.
The flow your `flatMap*` lambda returns for one outer value.
One inner flow being collected in its own coroutine. `concurrency` is the number of lanes.
Results leave in the order they finish, not the order their inputs arrived.
Pairs the n-th value of one flow with the n-th value of another, and ends with the shorter.
Keeps the latest value of each flow and emits a combination whenever any of them changes.
Interleaves several flows in arrival order and ends when the last one ends.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate's fee fan-out uses `flatMapMerge(concurrency = 8)`, yet the trace shows one pricing call at a time. Explain why, how you'd fix it, and how you'd keep one failing merchant from cancelling the rest. Use the toll plaza picture.
explain_back.answer: `flatMapMerge` has one dispatcher at the entrance: a single coroutine reads the merchants and calls the lambda for each, one at a time, before it waves the result into a booth. The booths are the 8 lanes, and only the flow the lambda returns is collected in a booth. The teammate does the pricing call in the lambda itself and returns `flowOf(fee)`, so the dispatcher inspects every car himself and the booths stay empty: one call at a time. The fix is to return `flow { emit(pricing.lookup(m)) }`, so the call runs inside the lane. To keep a 503 for one merchant from taking the others down, put `catch` on that inner flow and emit a default fee there. A `catch` after `flatMapMerge` comes too late, because the failing lane has already cancelled all the other lanes.

deeper.body:
How far does `flatMapMerge` run ahead of a slow collector? With 500 one-value inners and a collector stuck on its first value, 82 outer values had been pulled. A plausible split (my inference, not measured) is 64 results in the output channel, about 16 inners suspended on a full channel, and a couple in hand. With `.buffer(0)` after it the count was 18, and with `flatMapConcat` it was 1. So budget memory for up to 64 finished results plus `concurrency` inners. A `buffer` or `flowOn` after `flatMapMerge` fuses into the same channel: `flatMapMerge(4) { }.buffer(0)` prints as `ChannelFlowMerge[concurrency=4, capacity=0]`.

Edge cases: `flatMapMerge(1)` returns plain `flattenConcat()`. `flatMapMerge(0)` throws `IllegalArgumentException: Expected positive concurrency level, but had 0` when you build the flow. Setting `-Dkotlinx.coroutines.flow.defaultConcurrency=0` makes the first read of `DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY` throw `ExceptionInInitializerError`, caused by `IllegalStateException: System property 'kotlinx.coroutines.flow.defaultConcurrency' should be in range 1..2147483647, but is '0'`. With `=4`, 40 lookups of 100 ms took 1,000 ms instead of 300.

`flattenConcat()` and `flattenMerge()` are the same operators for a `Flow<Flow<T>>` you already have; `flatMapX(f)` is literally `map(f).flattenX()`.

The `flatMapMerge` and `flatMapConcat` KDoc both say they are discouraged in regular application flows, because "suspending operation in map operator will be sufficient and linear transformations are much easier to reason about". Take that at face value: reach for `flatMapMerge` when you need bounded concurrency, and for `map { suspendCall(it) }` when you don't.

`combineTransform` is `combine` with a `FlowCollector` receiver, so the transform can emit zero or several values per board update. Failure works the same way in `combine` and `merge`: one source that throws cancels the others (they end with `JobCancellationException: Parent job is Cancelling`) and the caller gets the original exception.
